title: History of the world's tallest structures

rows: Possibly one of the earliest known temples.
Tower of Jericho, West Bank, Palestine
One of the earliest ever stone monuments.
First Egyptian pyramid, formed of six stacked mastabas.
Shortly after completion Meidum Pyramid collapsed due to bad design/instability and is now 65 m (213 ft).
Angle of slope decreased during construction to avoid collapse.
Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt
It was destroyed by a lightning strike in 534. Its exact height is unknown, and estimates range from 137 m (in which case the Great Pyramid of Giza would have kept the record) to 240 m.
Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt
See also 2570 BC - 516 and 516 - 534. By 1647, the Great Pyramid's height had decreased to 139 m (456 ft) after its top was removed.
Old St Paul's Cathedral in London, England
The spire was destroyed by a lightning strike in 1561. Its height is disputed, for example by Christopher Wren (1632–1723), who suggested a height of 140 m (460 ft). [ 5 ]
The central spire was destroyed in a storm in 1548. While the reputed height of 525 ft (160 m) is accepted by most sources, [ 6 ] [ 7 ] [ 8 ] [ 9 ] [ 10 ] [ 11 ] others consider it doubtful [ 12 ]
St. Mary's Church in Stralsund, Germany
Spire collapsed in 1573; today, the church stands at a height of 67.2 metres (220.5 ft).
St. Mary's Church in Stralsund, Germany
See also 1548–1569. The church tower's spire burnt down after a lightning strike in 1647. Today the tower has a dome and stands at a height of 104 m (341 ft).
By 1647, the Pyramid of Khafre 's height had decreased from 143.5 m (471 ft) to 136.4 m (448 ft) after its top was removed.
The nave was demolished by aerial bombing during World War II; only the spire remains.
